items.en: Two Australian citizens were onboard a flight to Tel Aviv that was diverted after one of the pilots allegedly stabbed the other in an attack, according to the Israeli embassy.
The passengers are a Jewish couple from Sydney, the embassy in Australia confirmed to the Guardian on Thursday. No further details were provided.
The flydubai aircraft was travelling from the United Arab Emirates to Israel when it was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
One of the pilots, whom Israeli officials said was an Omani citizen, is accused of stabbing his co-pilot. During the alleged attack, the plane plunged about 17,000 feet in just two minutes.

Passenger Yaniv Hayoun later recounted how he and other passengers heard screaming and felt pressure as the plane dived before forcing their way into the cockpit and finding the attacker at the instrument panel.

“I grabbed the attacker, put him in a chokehold, and dragged him out first,” Hayoun said during a meeting with Netanyahu after the plane had landed safely and the passengers were flown to Israel. “He was trying to destroy the instruments to disable the plane.”
Israel’s ambassador to Australia, Hillel Newman, said the incident reminded him of the 11 September attacks.
“You have here a very special incident, and due to the real heroism of some people on board, they were saved.”
Newman said heightened security alerts had been issued following the attack.
“It just shows that … those that hate Israel also hate the peace.
“It’s an attempt to hit at the peace itself, at the Abraham Accords, and the relationships which Israel does have with Arab and Muslim countries.”
The Abraham Accords normalised relations between the UAE and Israel in 2020.
Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said it was too early to tell who was ultimately behind the the incident.
There are about 12,000 Australian citizens living in Israel and 25,000 in the UAE.
Dramatic video shows an Arizona sheriff's helicopter crew rescuing a man stranded on top of his overturned truck as rapidly moving floodwaters surrounded the vehicle.

The Maricopa County Sheriff's Office said its Fox 1 aviation crew responded Tuesday morning to a flooded wash in Tonopah, where deputies found the man sitting atop the overturned vehicle with water rushing around him.
Video released by authorities shows the man perched on the truck as muddy floodwaters rush past him.
Because of the dangerous conditions, first responders determined that directly reaching the man was too risky and decided a "hoist rescue" would be the safest option.
The video shows a Fox 1 crew member being lowered to the vehicle to secure the man in a rescue harness before both are hoisted to safety.
The man was taken to the riverbank, where fire personnel were waiting, according to the sheriff's office.
The helicopter's pilot, Rich Dickner, told CBS News that the water was quickly rising around the vehicle.
"We didn't waste much time," Dickner said.
"As opposed to when we first got there, you can see the water line on the video — it's below the window — and it had risen up to the top of the window," he continued. "So there was that urgency."
People Magazine reported that Deputy Lindsey Smith was lowered approximately 80 feet from the helicopter toward the overturned truck.
She initially struggled to get her footing before securing herself to the vehicle, according to the report.
The entire rescue took less than five minutes, authorities said.
The Maricopa County Sheriff's Office credited the crew's swift response with getting the man to safety.
"Thanks to the skill and quick response of our Aviation crew, the subject was safely brought to shore," the sheriff's office said.
The Weather Channel reported that remnants of Hurricane Polo brought historic rainfall to parts of the Desert Southwest, contributing to dangerous flash flooding.
The Flood Control District of Maricopa County warned drivers not to attempt to cross flooded roads.
"Remember: Conditions can change fast. If you encounter a flooded roadway, Turn Around, Don't Drown."
Fox News Digital has reached out to the Maricopa County Sheriff's Office for additional information.
Wednesday afternoon had plenty of potential for drama, with all four wild card series offering the potential for teams to advance into the division round of the Major League Baseball playoffs.

The first game of the quadruple-header, the Atlanta Braves and Philadelphia Phillies, delivered in spades. A Bryce Harper misplay in the 7th inning allowed two Braves' runs to score, putting the Phillies on the brink of elimination. But Schwarber and Harper hit back-to-back homers in the 8th to tie it, and a 10th inning homer for Alec Bohm won it for Philadelphia to force a winner-take-all game three on Thursday.

Then there's the Houston Astros. The Astros entered game two needing a win to force a game three, sending their ace, Hunter Brown, to the mound against the White Sox' powerful lineup. 36 pitches, five hits, four runs, two errors and just two outs later, the White Sox had a 4-0 lead and Brown was out of the game.

That summed up Houston's series; just not quite good enough to overcome Chicago's offense. The White Sox, one of baseball's most strikeout-prone offenses, had 13 in Wednesday's game, but kept chipping away, fending off an attempted Astros comeback with a massive three-run homer from Chase Meidroth in the 6th inning to give them some breathing room.

Four combined innings from Jordan Hicks and Erick Fedde closed it out to send the White Sox through for a massive ALDS against their division rival Cleveland Guardians. But they weren't done with the entertainment quite yet.
In the postgame clubhouse celebrations, star first year third baseman Munetaka Murakami gave what might be the quote of the season. When asked how he felt, Murakami answered, "100."
A minute later, after being joined by another member of the White Sox staff, Murakami, covered in beer, added, "I'm drunk, I'm drunk. Yesterday, maybe hungover, you know?"
After the interviewer offered a gentle correction, he said, "No, not yesterday, tomorrow. Sorry, I don't speak English."

Meanwhile, on the other side of the American League postseason bracket, the New York Yankees had an opportunity to sweep the hated Boston Red Sox after a dominant 9-0 win in game one. And after Cam Schlittler's remarkable outing on Tuesday, Max Fried was nearly as good on Wednesday.

Six innings with just one run allowed, three hits, one walk and six strikeouts, enough for New York to take a 2-1 lead into the bottom of the sixth. Which is where everything imploded for Boston. Garrett Crochet, making his first appearance on a big league mound since late-April, took over, hoping to keep the Yankees at two.

Instead, Spencer Jones reached on a strikeout, then stole second and advanced to third on a throwing error from catcher Adley Rutschmann. George Lombard singled in a run, Jazz Chisholm poked one through the right side, Trent Grisham got a bunt down for a hit, knocking Crochet out of the game without getting an out. Garrett Whitlock came in to stop the bleeding, but after two more runs scored on a sac fly and groundout, Cody Bellinger delivered the big blow.
On a 1-0 changeup, Bellinger took advantage of the short right field porch and knocked in three to make it 8-1.
New York cruised home with a 9-2 win, setting up an ALDS matchup with the Tampa Bay Rays.

There are a few big takeaways from these two sweeps, namely the importance of power in October baseball. It's an old adage that small ball wins against quality pitching, but it was the homers from Chicago in game one and two that gave them the edge, while Bellinger's bomb effectively put the game out of reach in the Bronx. Even without Aaron Judge, the Yankees' lineup outscored Boston 17-2. And with two days off before the start of the ALDS, Schlittler will be able to start in game two of the ALDS, with Gerrit Cole or Carlos Rodon available for game one.

While the Yankees are through, the other three teams left in the AL bracket are the Guardians, Rays and White Sox. Those teams rank 25th, 26th and 28th in total payroll respectively. There's a long ways to go to reach or win the World Series, but it's a bit of a tough look for MLB that the league office has spent the past few months preparing to lock players out by claiming that small market teams with low payrolls have no hope of meaningful baseball.
Pretty sure those three organizations should have hope. Saturday in Cleveland and Tampa should be a blast. Playoff baseball always is.
The Atlanta Dream avoided a first-round playoff exit for the first time in four years.

Atlanta, which finished with the Eastern Conference’s best regular-season record, had little trouble dispatching the Washington Mystics in Game 2 of their first-round WNBA playoff series Tuesday night. Star guard Allisha Gray led the Dream with 22 points in the 83-75 victory, punching Atlanta’s ticket to the semifinals for the first time since 2018.

Atlanta’s postseason run will continue Sunday, when the Dream host Game 1 of the semifinals against New York. The Liberty made league history by sweeping Minnesota, becoming the first No. 8 seed to eliminate a No. 1 seed in the league's 30-year history.

Jordin Canada made 3-pointers on back-to-back possessions in the fourth quarter, and she added a jumper from the free-throw line on Atlanta’s next trip for an 89-70 lead with just under three minutes left on the clock.

Rhyne Howard, the top pick in the 2022 WNBA Draft, ended the night with 15 points before fouling out with just over six minutes remaining in the fourth quarter. Angel Reese also had 15 points and seven rebounds.
The Mystics committed 11 first-half turnovers.
Washington went on a 14-2 run starting in the third quarter to get within 65-62. But Atlanta scored the next 13 points, capped by a 3-pointer by Canada, to rebuild a double-digit lead at 78-62.

The Mystics were making their first playoff appearance since winning the 2019 WNBA championship, while the Dream have captured the conference title three times from 2010-13 but have never won a WNBA championship.
The Dallas Wings hosted the Golden State Valkyries in Wednesday's other first-round series matchup.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Swiss glaciers suffer another year of record ice loss

BERN, Switzerland — Switzerland's glaciers lost more than 5% of their ice in 2026, marking another year of rapid decline. The loss reflects a wider global trend: Glaciers around the world have been shrinking at increasingly rapid rates, a phenomenon scientists link directly to global warming.

Matthias Huss leads Switzerland's glacier monitoring network, known as GLAMOS, which released the report alongside the Swiss Academy of Sciences (SCNAT). Each summer, Huss heads high into the mountains to measure the country's ice fields. For years, his research has documented rapid ice loss, with the decline peaking in 2022, when Switzerland recorded a record 6% loss in a single year.
At the end of this year's long, hot summer, Huss returned to some of the glaciers to find much of the ice gone.
"They are completely devoid of ice," he said. "It's a moon landscape that is dry and dead. There are some little remnants, some ice blocks still lying around and melting there on the hot rocks."

In other places, alpine plants are now seeding themselves in areas once covered by glaciers that were meters thick. This year's glacier monitoring report shows the ice loss in 2026 is 5.5%, and the only reason it is slightly lower than 2022's record is because there was slightly more winter snow covering the ice.
Ominously, though, Huss' research shows that individual glaciers, among them Switzerland's biggest, like the mighty Rhône and Aletsch, have suffered record ice loss this year.

Why is this important? Because these huge ice fields are often called Europe's water towers. They store winter snow and release it gently as it melts over the spring and summer. That snowmelt fills Europe's key waterways, like the Rhine and the Danube. The water is key to Europe's food supply, and much more.

"It's the food supply, it's the transportation chains," says Huss. This summer, as river levels sank, freight transport in the Rhine and Danube came to a standstill, and nuclear power stations, cooled by river water, had to be temporarily shut down.

This situation can only get worse if the melt continues. Although Europe's rivers did have some water this summer, it came not from seasonal snowmelt, but from the glaciers themselves melting. Once they are gone — and 1,200 smaller glaciers have disappeared in the last 50 years — drought could pose an existential threat to Europe's farmers.

There are other threats too. Glaciers and alpine permafrost are key to stability; they are a kind of glue that holds the mountains together. Without that glue, the risk of landslides and even flooding increases. Last year, the Swiss village of Blatten was wiped out when a fragile glacier crashed down, bringing the side of the mountain with it and destroying 300 homes.

Fortunately, the instability was being monitored, and Blatten's population was evacuated before the landslide. But one year later, they are still living in temporary accommodation, with no idea if they will ever be able to return to homes now buried under an estimated 9 million cubic meters of ice, rock and mud.
This summer, on Nepal's border with Tibet, the collapse of a glacier triggered devastating floods that killed at least 1,400 people.

Matthias Huss is cautious about making a direct link between climate change and such disasters. Mountain environments, he points out, have always been risky. "It's a bit more complicated than just saying it's warm and the glaciers are disappearing, so the mountains are falling apart and causing disasters like this," he explains.

But, he adds, climate change can be the catalyst for such natural disasters. "Combined with this heat, with the disappearance of the ice, with the warming of permafrost, climate change can be a triggering factor. That can just be the last bit that is missing to trigger such events."

And after years of monitoring the glaciers, Huss has little patience with those who still claim climate change does not exist. What is happening to the glaciers should be a warning sign, he argues. "Look at them, it's not a hoax. The evidence is clear, and it's been clear for decades. And I think many people have understood that it's time to act now."

Without action, Europe's beloved alpine landscape could, quite soon, look very different. If the planet keeps warming at its current rate, the glacier monitoring unit predicts, all the glaciers will be gone by the end of this century.
Greetings from Syria, where time seems to melt as a glassmaker braves scorching temps
Our world as journalists can move fast; every day there's breaking news from all corners of the world, and we scramble to stay on top of multiple threads of information each day.

That is why I loved watching this glassmaker just outside the historic Old City in Damascus. In 100 degree summer heat, he patiently shaped cup after glass cup in the blistering furnace in front of him, seemingly impervious to the temperature.

Time seemed to matter less than the process of melting and stretching the hot, melted glass. He made cups and oil jars and decorative lamps in a variety of jewel colors, using techniques and styles that have not changed for decades. Watching his craft reminded me to slow down and enjoy the moment, too.

Even though his shop was right on the edge of the Old City of Damascus, it was largely empty. Syria's nearly 14-year civil war has ended, but the economy is still struggling, while inflation has ratcheted up the cost of living in the last year. Even a glass can be a luxury for some.

How Ukrainians are coping with new, more deadly Russian attacks
Zanny Minton Beddoes, The Economist's editor in chief, just visited Ukraine. She says, despite all its drone weaponry, Kyiv is under extraordinary bombardment, as Russia tries to make it unlivable.

This is FRESH AIR. I'm Dave Davies. Since Russia invaded Ukraine 4 1/2 years ago, Ukrainian forces have held their own on the battlefield with support from Western allies, and morale among the country's civilian population has held up, despite punishing air attacks. But our guest, Zanny Minton Beddoes, editor in chief of The Economist, says the war is changing in ways that bring a new level of terror to Ukrainian citizens and pose serious threats to the country's economy.

Minton Beddoes recently returned from a reporting trip with a team of journalists to Ukraine, where, she says, both sides in the war are developing new weapons and refining tactics with lethal consequences. One example, so-called safari hunting drones that identify a person or vehicle as a target, then follow as the target flees in terror. The drone eventually dives and crashes into the target, detonating a deadly explosive charge. We've invited Zanny Minton Beddoes back on the show to talk about Ukraine and catch up on some other important topics, including the war with Iran, trade, tariffs and the state of U.S., European and Canadian alliances.

Zanny Minton Beddoes is a former economist for the International Monetary Fund who joined The Economist magazine in 1994. She holds degrees from Oxford University and Harvard University and is a regular commentator on television and radio. We recorded our conversation yesterday.
Zanny Minton Beddoes, welcome back to FRESH AIR.
ZANNY MINTON BEDDOES: Thank you so much for having me.

DAVIES: You and this team of journalists from the economist recently made an extensive trip to Ukraine. You've been there before. Why did you feel you wanted to make this kind of investment in this subject now?

MINTON BEDDOES: So you're right. I've been there four times since the invasion by Russia, the full-scale invasion - the first, I think, three weeks after the invasion, when I went to Kyiv and was the first journalist to interview President Zelenskyy. The reason I go is because I think this is the most important geopolitical conflict in Europe in, you know, the last 70 years. And I actually have a kind of personal soft spot for Ukraine. I lived there for a few months 30 years ago. I find it a fascinating country. And I - you know, I feel that you can only really understand something, particularly a conflict like that, if you actually see it close up.

And I have to say, Dave, this is a very sobering trip. And it was probably the most sobering since the very first time I went, which was, the first time, in 2022. The Russians were still just outside Kyiv. The city was virtually empty. You know, we went to see President Zelenskyy kind of in bunkers. And, I mean, it was in his palace, but there were sandbags everywhere. It really felt like a place at war. But the subsequent two times, when I went to Kyiv, it felt like a normal city. The war felt far away because the city then had very good air defenses. And, yes, there were occasional air alerts, but you felt as though you were in a very safe city.

This time around, I went to Kyiv, and then I went to visit the brigade headquarters of one of the drone brigades, much closer to the front, in a location that I'm obviously not going to disclose, but much closer to the front. And Kyiv itself - and this is, I think, really important for people to understand - in the last couple of months, but really the last few weeks, has been under extraordinary bombardment from the Russians. And they are basically trying to make life unlivable in a city of several million people.

And there are two big things that have changed that have given the Russians an advantage. The first is that the Ukrainians have run out of interceptors for ballistic missiles, what are called PAC-3 interceptors produced by the U.S., which for the past couple of years have really helped them to defend themselves against ballistic missiles. And because these interceptors are in extremely short supply - they were used heavily in the Middle East recently in the Iran War - the Ukrainians have essentially hardly got any left. So the Russians are able to bombard the city at night with ballistic missiles.

And the second is that the Russians have made an innovation to their drones. Their kind of workhorse drone is something called the Shahed drone, which was originally made by Iran, that the Russians started producing at scale. And they have essentially attached jet propulsion to those drones, which makes them go much higher and much faster and thus makes them much harder for the Ukrainians to intercept. And Ukrainians had built sort of defensive drones that could intercept the Shaheds with a sort of 95% success rate. But now that they have these jet propulsion attached to them, that interception rate has gone down closer to 40%, and the Russians have enormous quantities of these drones that they are just sending into Ukraine, essentially, all day and all night now.
DAVIES: What does that mean day to day for civilians who are used to air raid sirens, right? I mean, this is not like they're not used to living in a wartime.

MINTON BEDDOES: So I think the difference is that, you know - if you're living in Kyiv, you have an app on your phone. And I had it on my phone when I was there. And it goes off every time there is a you know, ballistic missile or a jet Shahed close - within, you know, a few, I think 50 or 100 kilometers. And basically, it's going off the whole time. And you are trying to live a normal life. And so you're looking, and you become normalized to this quite quickly, and you look at it and you say, well, is it likely to be in my part of town? Looks not too far away, so I'll - you know, if it's too close, you might go to a shelter. You might just keep an eye on it. But increasingly, it's happening all day, and you're suddenly discovering that the Metro isn't working. You're unable to get your kids from school. There's been an attack. A supermarkets blown up, you know. And every day, people are killed.
DAVIES: You paid a visit to the operation center of an elite drone unit in the Ukrainian army. Share with us what you saw there.

MINTON BEDDOES: So Ukraine has several of these unarmed systems brigades, as they're called, which are units that specialize in drones. And they were set up often by civilians, technologists, sort of separate from the army structure, but they work with the army structure. And they are in the vanguard of what this war is about, particularly at the front lines. And it is very different from what you imagine, you know, warfare to be from the movies. A drone-based war is one where the actual front lines - there are no people visible. There is what Ukrainians call the kill zone, which is now something like 20 to 30 kilometers each way from the contact line, where, essentially, anything that moves will be shot down, shot at by a drone within seconds or minutes.

MINTON BEDDOES: Yes, from both sides. There are hundreds of drones in the air - surveillance drones, drones, attack drones. That means that nothing can really move. So the few people who are there on both sides are, you know, in underground dugouts. They are often supplied by drone, or they're supplied by unmanned ground vehicles, essentially kind of robots on wheels. It's a dystopian hellscape. To be clear, I wasn't anywhere near there. I was sort of close to it, but well out of that area.

Then these drones are manned and sort of piloted by people in the brigade headquarters of the sort that I went to. They have huge screens, and it's like a cross between a sort of dystopian video game and a startup. There are huge numbers of computer screens. There are people who are plotting where the Russians - assets are. They are sending surveillance drones to go and find them. Then they're sending in drones to attack them. And the other side is doing that, too. And the area around the front line is now basically a sort of no-man's-land where nothing can move. And, you know, the Ukrainians are clearly trying to disrupt Russian supply lines by attacking well beyond the front lines. And then, of course, they're also increasingly hitting refineries much further into Russia. So this is a - on both sides, a drone-based war, whose characteristics are very, very fast innovation.

DAVIES: And I mentioned in the introduction, these so-called safari drones, where a pilot located somewhere is looking at what the drone sees. They identify a target - might be a person, might be a vehicle - and essentially kind of track them from the air as if they're a safari hunter and then smash the drone into the target, blow up a charge, right?

MINTON BEDDOES: That's exactly - and that's what happens on the front line in this kill zone the whole time. What is sort of newer is that the Russians are doing the same thing to attack civilians in front-line towns, and increasingly and alarmingly, they have the capability to reach bigger cities, potentially Kyiv, with this kind of drone, too. So the notion of safari-hunting individuals to kill them is now no longer some sort of dystopian fantasy. It's something that can happen.

DAVIES: The dreadful video that I've seen of a man, who - and there's this drone buzzing around above him, you know, six or eight feet in the air, and he's dodging around, trying to get behind a truck to kind of avoid it. And eventually, the drone dives into him, and he wasn't killed, but he was seriously injured. But just seeing it just seems - is utterly terrifying.

MINTON BEDDOES: It is. And what was really sobering to me is it was tough enough seeing all of this at this sort of center of this war. But what I realized is that these are tactics and capabilities that can be used by the Russians elsewhere. And if you remember just a few weeks ago, there was a narrow escape at Leipzig Airport when there was an attack, which - a drone was attacking a cargo plane at the airport. It was foiled, but it was in Germany, and the German government has said that the Russians were behind it. And I think there was realization for me, and in one of the conversations I had with the senior people at this drone brigade - became clear to me that their view is, these are the capabilities that the Russians have. Don't think that they're going to be confined just to Ukraine.

And I think there is a growing concern amongst European politicians and intelligence services that there will be more of this. We've had alarms raised from the Polish government. We've had alarms raised from Balkan governments. We've had alarms raised across the board that the Russians may well be planning to do more of this. And what became clear to me is that it is technologically totally doable now.

DAVIES: We need to take a break here. Let me reintroduce you. We are speaking with Zanny Minton Beddoes. She is editor in chief for The Economist. We'll continue our conversation in just a moment. This is FRESH AIR.
(SOUNDBITE OF LOS SUPER SEVEN SONG, "CALLE DIECISEIS")

DAVIES: This is FRESH AIR, and our guest today is The Economist's editor in chief, Zanny Minton Beddoes. We're looking at the war in Ukraine, and we'll be discussing some other topics, including the conflict in the Middle East and the state of Western alliances. Our interview was recorded yesterday.

You know, the Ukrainians have been effective in sending drones, behind the lines in Russia and attacking, you know, military infrastructure, energy infrastructure. And one of the ways that they have been able to operate it is by using these Starlink satellite hookups, which are, you know, operated by SpaceX, Elon Musk's company. I understand that Musk does not let Ukraine use those for attacks inside Russia. Is that right?

MINTON BEDDOES: Yes, that's right. Starlink is available to the Ukrainians over Ukrainian territory, including the territory that is Ukrainian, but the Russians are occupying. But it is not available to them over Russia. And what that means is that the Ukrainians lack the ability to go after the launch sites, for example, for ballistic missiles. So there is a huge plea from the Ukrainians to the Americans to basically push SpaceX to allow them to have access to Starlink over Russian territory so that they can go after the launch sites from which these ballistic missiles are raining down on them.

Interestingly and alarmingly, something that I hadn't really focused on until I went to Ukraine and sort of really delved into this, the Russians have been and are building their own version of Starlink called Rassvet, which is still in its early stages. However, after months of tensions, New Delhi is adopting a more openly critical tone towards Washington to address the volatility and uncertainty that Trump brings to the White House.

The changing tune in New Delhi also comes at a critical time for Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who faces mounting domestic pressure and criticism from the opposition for allegedly bowing down to US pressure, time and again. On Wednesday, Modi held a telephone call with Trump, which the Indian PM called “productive” — a cold and formal depiction far removed from his description of the US president as a “good friend” in previous years.

Chietigj Bajpaee, a senior research fellow for South Asia at the Chatham House think tank, said that Jaishankar’s remarks “offer a frank assessment” on the current state of the India-US relationship. “Clearly, the shine has come off the bilateral relationship after India was initially among the most optimistic about a second Trump term,” he said.
Jaishankar addressed frictions between India and the US while speaking at an Asia Society event after the UN General Assembly in New York ended on Monday.

“If I stand back and look at the [India-US] relationship, I note that much of the world has had a more difficult relationship with the US,” he said. “I mean that may not be a consolation, but that’s a reality.”

Trade has been one of the flashpoints. Washington is India’s largest trading partner, with bilateral goods trade reaching $149.1 billion in 2025; but the relationship remains tilted towards India with a $58.4 billion goods surplus.
Jaishankar started by noting: “Countries should not be so self-centred that you’re in your own world and take your decision and say, ‘Well, it was not my intention to make your life difficult’.”
The minister was partly referring to the economic spillover of the wars in Iran and Ukraine, urging that “sound common sense” should ensure that the basic needs of countries were not neglected.

But then, he referred to the trade negotiations between India and the US, that have so far yielded a roadmap to a deal — but not a deal itself. “Apart from the per capita gap between India and the United States, the nature of production and the nature of society is very different,” he noted.

The agricultural sector has been among the most contested points between the two, where India has kept its market largely closed for decades to safeguard its farmers. “The expectation that it could rapidly move forward was tested against the ground reality, which was much more complex,” he said, adding that “there is more or less an understanding on the trade agreement.”

At one point, India was among the countries facing the worst tariff rates imposed by Trump. After the US Supreme Court struck down Trump’s sweeping tariffs in February, his administration swiftly turned to other tools, including a new 10 percent global tariff. Earlier this month, Trump signed a law under which the US can impose up to 100 percent tariffs on countries like India that purchase Russian oil.

Jaishankar pointed to these changes, noting that the negotiations created “bumps last year for the relationship,” and added that once the deal is closed, it “would contribute to a better relationship.”

Ajay Bisaria, a retired diplomat who served as high commissioner to Canada and Pakistan, and as ambassador to Poland, told Al Jazeera that with Washington, in particular, “India has decided to be more public because there has been a lot of public criticism and a sentiment that the US is bullying India and India has been silent.”

The new 100 percent tariff on India, due to come into effect in less than a month, “is sort of a deal breaker in the relationship right now,” said Bisaria. “If that becomes reality, then all Indian efforts [to reach out to the US] would come under scrutiny.”

But trade isn’t the only challenge in the relationship. A major rupture emerged in May last year, when New Delhi engaged in a four-day war with its bitter neighbour, Pakistan, after an attack by armed fighters in Indian-administered Kashmir killed 26 civilians.

New Delhi was upstaged as President Trump announced a ceasefire, claiming that he threatened both countries with economic damage if they didn’t stop fighting. For India, any question on Kashmir is strictly bilateral with Pakistan, with no room for so-called third-party intervention.

Nevertheless, Trump has gone on to claim dozens of times that he brokered the crucial ceasefire — as recently as at the UNGA in New York — that halted the war between two nuclear-armed neighbours. India took offence to these claims.

On the other hand, Pakistan’s leaders cozied up to Trump, showered high praise, and nominated him for a Nobel Peace Prize. Since then, the relationship between Islamabad and Washington has bloomed, to New Delhi’s obvious irk.
For India, Jaishankar said, “particularly important is the issue of terrorism.”

“As a country, perhaps there are very few countries which have been subjected to the kind of terrorism that we have from a neighbour as part of a deliberate, conscious policy over many, many decades,” Jaishankar said, referring to Pakistan.

“Now, if something which matters so deeply to us, there isn’t enough understanding or appreciation or empathy of that, I think that creates a problem too,” he said, adding that India’s primary concerns are “not fully appreciated” by its partner, the US.

New Delhi’s changing tone while addressing Washington “is a lesson learnt from its experiences,” said Bisaria, the former diplomat. “After the ceasefire issue, the moods changed — and it all became worse.”

Harsh Pant, vice president of the Observer Research Foundation, a New Delhi-based think tank, said that “the obsession with Pakistan in the Trump administration without taking India’s sensitivities into account contributed to the sense that, look, we need to start articulating it.”
“When at the top level, you don’t see reciprocity, then calculations change and decisions are taken to bring differences out in the open,” Pant told Al Jazeera, referring to Jaishankar’s comments.

Indians have been the biggest beneficiaries of the US’s H1B programme which allows hiring of foreign workers with training in specialty fields. But that has come under fire from Trump, under whose watch Washington has raised barriers and fees for applicants, amid growing criticism of the scheme from supporters of his MAGA movement.

“For many years, mobility was seen as an economic gain. Today the economics of mobility and the politics of mobility are at odds with each other, at least in some quarters,” Jaishankar said, referring to Trump’s anti-immigration politics.
“That certainly in public perception is an issue,” the minister said.

Domestic pressure appears to be finally catching up in New Delhi. “Modi is feeling domestic pressure, with key state elections coming up next year, especially amid some anti-incumbency,” said Bisaria. “It dictates that the government’s posture should not be one of taking bullying from the US.”

Pant said issues like migration impact the general public in India, with the world’s largest population. For years, such connections made the US “an attractive partner for a large mass of Indians.” But today, he said, ”the same issues are becoming a negative drag on the relationship.”
“The public mood in India is also changing perceptibly towards the US. And I think the government is articulating that negative sentiment now publicly,” Pant said.

When Trump returned to the White House for his second presidential run, many in New Delhi’s strategic community were optimistic about bilateral relations, because of the US president’s warm personal relations with PM Modi during his first term.
But things unravelled in the coming months.
Still, Chatham House’s Bajpaee said that despite widening divisions between the US and India, “both have not given up on reviving their relationship”.

He pointed to Jaishankar’s remarks that India isn’t singled out in having a difficult relationship with the US. “Rather, the downturn in India-US relations is a reflection of the Trump administration’s transactional and often unpredictable or erratic foreign policy,” he told Al Jazeera.
“This offers a potential off-ramp for an eventual reset in relations. The conclusion of a bilateral trade agreement is a key watchpoint for this,” Bajpaee added.
For New Delhi, Pant said, “it is now just the question of waiting Mr. Trump out.” Though he added, with a laugh, that India is not alone in that queue.
“Everyone is waiting him out. President Trump has little respect for conventions and norms of inter-state behaviour. How do you just deal with that individual?” Pant said.

A new report on conditions in the Gaza Strip says that the roughly 1.8 million Palestinians in Gaza, or 86% of the population, living in displacement sites often face inhumane living conditions.

The Danish Refugee Council (DRC) published its findings on Thursday, almost three years after the October 7 terror attacks against Israel that triggered the war in Gaza, and a year after the phased October 10 ceasefire plan that was supposed to usher in the war's end.

"The October 2025 ceasefire in Gaza was supposed to end civilians' suffering. Nearly a year on, it exists largely in name only. Displacement in Gaza has not ended; it has changed shape," the report says.
The findings are based on group discussions with 195 people living in internal displacement camps across five governorates in Gaza.
What did the DRC say about the Yellow Line?
Entitled "Confined by Design: The Human Cost of Protracted Displacement in Gaza," the report accuses Israel of "a policy of protracted displacement" since the ceasefire deal was reached.

One means of ensuring this, the DRC says, is the so-called "Yellow Line," which demarcates the area of eastern Gaza near the border that is controlled by the Israeli military and is, according to the report, creeping toward the coast.

"In addition to protracted displacement for hundreds of thousands of people, the defining feature of the so-called ceasefire is the Yellow Line which continues expanding westward and swallowing up more land, effectively squeezing families into 30% of Gaza's territory," said the NGO's country director for the occupied Palestinian territories, Alan Moseley.
Other groups, including the UN, have also reported the westward movement of the Yellow Line, as has the Israeli government, although some details differ.
Last month, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu put the share of Gaza's territory inside the Yellow Line at 60% rather than 70%, but he also said the plan was to expand the area.
The DRC report also said aid organizations "describe being unable to operate within several kilometers of the line, either due to access constraints or security concerns."
It said that this led to crucial aid and supplies failing to reach displacement camps nearer the boundary.
What did the report say about living conditions in displacement camps?

The DRC and the Agricultural Development Association (PARC) highlighted a series of major shortcomings in the often informal tent shelters and makeshift camps that have sprung up amid Gaza's rubble, where more than eight in 10 residents are believed to be living.
- 80% of respondents reporting shortages of water both for washing and drinking
- Displaced households relying on outdoor cesspits
- Multiple families sharing single latrines, increasing the risk of gender-based violence and abuse
- Rat and rodent infestations exacerbated by the unsanitary conditions
- Food scarcity and lacking infrastructure for cooking, increasing risks of burns or injury preparing meals
- Rapid localized spread of illnesses and infections. For instance, more than 4,000 chickenpox cases were recorded in Khan Younis displacement camps in July alone
- Lacking and overburdened medical facilities with only half of hospitals and just over a third of primary healthcare centers still operational
- Lacking or non-existent formal education provision for young people, now lasting almost three years in some cases
- Reports of security concerns, particularly among men, because of the continued presence of artillery strikes, drones and stray gunfire
- Safety risks posed by unexploded and undiscovered ordnance, particularly when trying to clear rubble or return to areas where people originally lived
The Danish Refugee Council also laid particular emphasis on lacking site management mechanisms at displacement camps.
It said only 36% of sites currently had a designated site manager, typically a national NGO, coordinating services and managing conditions.

Sites with such partners "have a structured community channel through which a gap, such as a collapsing cesspit, a missing water delivery, or an unsafe walkway, can be identified, escalated, and resolved," the report said.
Israel has not yet commented on the newly released report.

The DRC and PARC issued a number of appeals and recommendations, some to "all parties to the conflict," most to "the Government of Israel, as the occupying power of Gaza" and others to "the international community" and "donors and humanitarian actors."
- Completely upholding pledges to cease hostilities
- Ending attacks against civilians, humanitarian workers and medical personnel
- Guaranteeing humanitarian access and medical evacuation pathways
- Supporting the establishment of a UN mechanism to monitor ceasefire violations.
The groups called on Israel to "halt the further expansion of the Yellow Line" and to "disclose its current and future route transparently."
They also urged Israel to cease the construction of permanent military infrastructure in the area and to provide "credible assurance that current troop positions are not intended to be permanent."

They appealed for fewer restrictions on aid access, particularly so-called "dual-use" restrictions affecting medical supplies, water, sanitation and hygiene items, pest control, rubble removal and fuel.
The report also warned that political and donor interest in the situation had declined markedly in the year since the ceasefire, even though conditions had not improved proportionately.

Deportation centers are legally contentious, expensive and the subject of political controversy: For years, Brussels has been grappling with the issue of establishing such centers outside the EU for rejected asylum seekers. Previous attempts have failed due to legal objections, but now, a "group of five" consisting of Greece, Germany, Austria, Denmark and the Netherlands believes it has overcome these hurdles.

During an interview with the Greek television channel ANT1, Greece's Minister of Migration, Thanos Plevris, stated that the first of these so-called "return hubs" is scheduled to begin operations as early as the second half of 2027 — just in time for Greece to assume the EU Council Presidency.

Plevris said Greece had chosen an African country but could not reveal its name yet. Diplomatic circles and media outlets close to the EU have repeatedly cited Rwanda or Uganda, but neither country has been confirmed as the location.
"We are not talking about centers in the sense that someone whose asylum application is rejected is sent to a closed facility in a third country," Plevris said.
The plan was rather to establish "open facilities" while the final return to the actual country of origin is being organized, he added.

The responsibility for the transferred individuals will not be transferred to the African partner country in order to prevent legal action for human rights violations, but will remain with the five participating EU member states. The EU "group of five" will also finance the project entirely on its own.

There are also plans for international organizations such as the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) or the International Organization for Migration (IOM) to monitor operations to ensure that international human rights standards and principles of international law are upheld.

Various attempts have been made in recent years to outsource asylum proceedings or deportations to countries outside the EU. None of these models worked as planned. All failed due to legal impediments, changes in government, or high costs. Below are some of the best-known precedents.

The United Kingdom, under the Conservative government of Boris Johnson — and later under Rishi Sunak — sought to permanently deport migrants who had entered the country irregularly via the English Channel to Rwanda so they could undergo their asylum proceedings there.

However, the British Supreme Court ruled the plan illegal, finding that there were substantial grounds for believing that asylum seekers sent to Rwanda faced a real risk of refoulement — being returned to countries where they could face persecution or other inhumane treatment.

Prior to that, the British government had spent £715 million (€835 million/$966 million) in taxpayer funds on the Rwanda partnership and related implementation costs. In return, a total of four people had voluntarily relocated to Rwanda
Italy's Albania model (in place since 2024)

Under Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, Italy signed an agreement with Albania to transport migrants intercepted in the Mediterranean directly to Italian-run centers established in Albania where expedited asylum proceedings could be conducted.

However, immediately after the camps opened, Italian courts halted the relocation. Judges argued that countries of origin such as Bangladesh or Egypt should not be classified as "safe" outright if certain groups face persecution there. These first migrants had to be returned to Italy immediately.

Italy is now using one of the camps solely as a deportation center for men whose asylum applications in Italy have been definitively rejected. Since the facility was converted in March 2025, only about 500 people have been sent there. By 2028, this comes at an estimated total cost of more than €670 million ($775 million).
Denmark's stand-alone initiatives (2021–2023)

In 2021, Denmark passed a law intended to allow asylum seekers to be flown to third countries outside the EU. Copenhagen engaged in intensive negotiations with Rwanda regarding a dedicated reception center. However, the European Commission and human rights organizations sharply criticized the initiative. In early 2023, the Danish government put the negotiations with Rwanda on hold. It became clear that the Danish plan was virtually impossible to implement legally and logistically. The government subsequently moved toward pursuing third-country return arrangements in cooperation with other European countries.

According to previous EU law, deportations to third countries often failed as courts required that a migrant have a personal connection to that third country, whether through language skills, relatives living there or a previous stay. The revised European asylum law, however, now allows individuals required to leave the EU to be transferred to a safe third country without a prior personal connection in certain circumstances — provided there is a corresponding agreement or arrangement with the third country.

A further basis for this new joint effort is the EU Return Regulation, agreed upon politically on June 17, 2026 by the Council and European Parliament. However, the regulation has not yet been formally adopted by the Council. Unlike before, the new legislation is an EU regulation and no longer merely a directive. As a result, it will apply directly once it enters into force in the EU member states bound by it. The regulation thus establishes a common EU framework for such return centers.

Furthermore, according to the new plans, the entire asylum procedure will no longer be outsourced to non-EU countries. The United Kingdom and Italy rejected this proposal. Instead, these "return hubs" will serve solely as transit stations for individuals whose asylum applications have already been legally rejected while they are financed and monitored by EU member states.

Supporters hope that these measures will undermine the basis for human rights lawsuits regarding permanent asylum protection. Critics such as Doctors Without Borders and Amnesty International still see significant risks: They doubt that independent oversight, effective legal representation and medical care can be fully guaranteed in the hubs. They also fear that third countries could still deport people to their unsafe home countries without proper assessment.

Furthermore, experience to date shows that the construction and security of such centers, as well as the transport of those affected, often costs hundreds of millions of euro, and only a small number of people actually end up being returned.

After day of delays, witnesses say Tennessee unable to carry out execution of Christa Pike
Pike did not appear to die after authorities administered lethal injection doses

Tennessee officials were unable to carry out the execution of Christa Gail Pike for a 1995 murder on Wednesday, media witnesses said, after the lethal injection was halted for hours as courts considered a last-minute appeal.
Pike, 50, had been scheduled for execution after the U.S. Supreme Court overturned an appeals court ruling that stopped the lethal injection just an hour before it was to start.
Officials appeared to give Pike two doses of pentobarbital.
At 7:46 p.m. prison officials closed the curtain to the media room. They raised the curtain three minutes later. Pike could be heard loudly snoring, and the curtain was closed again at 8:06 pm.
Pike continued to be heard snoring behind the closed curtain until the microphone was cut off at about 8:53 p.m. At that time there was an announcement to escort media witnesses out of the area.
Tennessee Department of Correction spokesman Dorinda Carter told media witnesses she was unable to immediately provide information about what happened.

Lawyers for Pike filed an emergency motion late Wednesday to the U.S. Supreme Court seeking to immediately halt and stay the execution, saying she was in "unnecessary agony" and it was violating her right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment. They also filed motions in the Sixth Circuit court and district court.
The motion also asserted that the Department of Correction should begin lifesaving measures. "Failure to provide such care constitutes deliberate indifference to legitimate, serious medical needs."
Pike and her boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, were convicted of stabbing and beating 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, their classmate at a job training facility, in Knoxville in 1995.

The case garnered widespread attention in part because a pentagram that was carved on Slemmer's body and other elements of the crime stoked fears of Satan worship during the "satanic panic" of the 1980s and 1990s.

She was initially scheduled to die by lethal injection in the morning, and witnesses had already gathered at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville when the 6th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals voted 2-1 to issue a stay. That court said a delay was needed to consider whether Pike's allegations of childhood sexual abuse were fully considered at her sentencing.

But later in the day, the U.S. Supreme Court cleared the way for the execution to proceed. The Supreme Court's conservative majority did not explain their order, while the three liberal members signed a dissent that said Pike's claims deserved a closer look.
A spokesperson for the Tennessee Department of Correction then said it would proceed with the execution ahead of a midnight cutoff.
After the stay was issued, Tennessee's attorney general immediately appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court. Witnesses and media remained at the prison while the high court considered the case.

In its appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court, the attorney general's office wrote that halting the execution at the last moment traumatized Slemmer's family and rewarded "abusive delay tactics" by Pike's lawyers.

Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor wrote in the dissent that the decision to vacate the stay interfered with the Sixth Circuit court's handling of the case and "unnecessarily prevents that court from giving due consideration to Pike's claim."

Pike does not deny committing the killing, but her supporters have argued the state should consider her age at the time, mental illness and a history of severe sexual abuse that included being raped from the time she was a toddler.

"It is inconceivable that in the 21st century, the criminal justice system is poised to execute a survivor of rape and child sexual abuse whose jury never had the opportunity to consider those facts in weighing the defendant's moral culpability," her lawyers wrote in a filing to the U.S. Supreme Court.
As the execution date drew near, it renewed debate over the death penalty for young offenders.
Assistant Federal Defender Stephen Ferrell said Pike's death sentence is an outlier because other 18-year-olds sentenced to death in Tennessee have had their sentences vacated.

After the killing, Pike was diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder. In her clemency petition, she said she only wanted to fight Slemmer but killed her in a frenzied attack when she couldn't "put the brakes on."
"I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid. It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I'd done," Pike said in a statement included in her clemency petition.
"Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone's child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime."
Slemmer's mother wants the lethal injection to go forward, saying she has waited decades to see Pike's sentence carried out.
"Every time I think about it, I think about Colleen feeling that pain and trying to get up and run," May Martinez said in a telephone interview.
Martinez said a group helped raise money so she and her husband could travel from Florida to witness the execution. She didn't respond to a message on Wednesday after the execution was halted.
Martinez said her daughter's age also should matter in deciding Pike's fate.
"Not a day goes by, or a minute goes by that I do not think about Colleen. Holidays are the worst," Martinez said, noting that her daughter would have turned 51 earlier in September.
The 1995 killing rocked the city of Knoxville. Prosecutors said Pike, fearing Slemmer was trying to steal her boyfriend, lured her to a wooded area on Jan. 12, 1995.
Shipp was 17 when the crime happened and received a sentence of life in prison with the possibility of parole. Pike was the only one sentenced to death.

Tennessee has not executed a woman for at least 200 years, according to Robin M. Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center. Older records can be spotty, though, so it's difficult to know precise details about the last woman who was put to death there.
It's a rarity across the U.S. Since 1976, 18 women have been put to death in the country, representing about one per cent of all executions, according to the centre.
Most recently, Missouri in 2023 executed Amber McLaughlin for a 2003 killing, in what is believed to be the first execution of a transgender woman in the U.S.
In 2021, the federal government executed Lisa Montgomery, marking the first time in nearly seven decades that the U.S. government put a female inmate to death.
Pike would be the 30th person executed in the U.S. this year after Florida carried out an execution on Tuesday.

Captain Smit Machchhar was operating the Boeing 737 MAX 8 aircraft from Dubai to Tel Aviv on Wednesday when his co-pilot allegedly attacked him and "apparently tried to crash the plane", according to Israel's prime minister.
The plane reportedly entered a "tailspin", but according to passengers onboard and Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Captain Machchhar "fought back" and "resisted", despite his injuries.
He also managed to open the door to the cockpit, allowing a passenger and crew member to enter and subdue the co-pilot.
A second pair of off-duty flydubai pilots then landed the plane in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.
India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi has since hailed the Indian captain a "hero" and said India is "proud".
"In the face of the gravest danger and despite being seriously injured, he showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others," he said in a social media post.
Mr Netanyahu has also given a "salute" to the Indian pilot on social media site X, for his "extraordinary bravery".
"He saved the lives of 174 people, including Israeli citizens and other nationals," he said.
Leading news outlets in India have praised the pilot for his bravery, with The Times of India calling him a "hero".
Flydubai said in a statement that the underlying reasons for the event remained unknown. It has warned against "premature speculation".
Captain Machchhar is from Gujarat but his parents live in Mumbai, India's largest city, and its financial centre.
Local newspaper, the Mumbai Mirror, said his parents had left their home in the Tilak Nagar neighbourhood to travel to Saudi Arabia on Wednesday afternoon to be with their son.

Captain CS Randhawa from the Federation of Indian Pilots, a professional welfare organisation representing pilots, told the ABC he was waiting for an investigation report into what happened, but if media reports were correct and the co-pilot was trying to "take down the plane", then Captain Machchhar did a "miraculous job".
According to his LinkedIn, Captain Machchhar flew for SpiceJet Limited in Mumbai for more than 11 years, before joining flydubai four years ago.
In a statement the budget airline said his "SpiceJet family" joined "millions across the country and around the world" in wishing him a swift recovery.
"You are a hero to us all, Captain," the company wrote.
In his podcast interview, Captain Machchhar spoke about discovering an interest in flying during a management course at 19, saying the "aviation bug bit him".
He said his mum was initially "scared" of him flying.
Captain Machchhar completed his early flight training in New Zealand.

Indian newspaper, The Times of India, has reported multiple friends and colleagues referred to Captain Machchhar as a "great guy" with one senior pilot who trained him, describing him as "very decent".
Childhood friend and former neighbour Prateek Gandhi told Press Trust of India that Captain Machchhar was "very calm and composed" and the "least trouble-making kid in our society".
But like other friends and family, he is concerned about his recovery.
"We heard that he is doing good, operation done but other than this we have not seen news from the family," he said.
Vision filmed in the aftermath of the attack on Wednesday showed Captain Machchhar on the ground bleeding, wearing an oxygen mask.
An Israeli dentist who was onboard the flight rendered first aid, according to Israeli media.
"When I came into the cockpit, the pilot was in real bad shape, with heavy bleeding, particularly from his head," Dr Shota Musayev told the Times of Israel.
"I was the only doctor on the plane, and eventually I managed to stop the bleeding and stabilise his blood pressure."
Dr Musayev told CNN the pilot had suffered "massive blood loss" and was "severely wounded".
"He was covered in cuts — his head, his hands — they were practically sliced open, almost severed in two," he said.
The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia said Captain Machchhar had been taken to hospital and was now in a stable condition.
In an online statement, it said it was following the condition of the "brave pilot" with a "full update" on his health was to come.
"We hope that he recovers from his injuries at the earliest."
A bus service transporting passengers between remote communities and Alice Springs says NT government funding cuts could force them to halt five of their routes.
Local organisations say the service is critical and the loss of it could leave remote residents stuck in Alice Springs, staying in overcrowded homes.
The NT government says the service missed out on funding because its costs were not comparative with other services in the Territory.

Aboriginal people will be stranded in Alice Springs and forced to stay off country in overcrowded housing unless funding for a remote bus service is reinstated by the NT Government, according to local organisations.
Centre Bush Bus has been transporting people, critical medical supplies and goods to remote Indigenous communities from Alice Springs for three decades.
Earlier this week the organisation's owners said a funding cut at the end of February had forced the reduction of services on five routes across Central Australia, from two trips a week to just one.

Centre Bush Bus user Marlene Nampijinpa Spencer, who is from Kintore — a 10.5 hour drive from Alice Springs — said while her route had not been cut, a reduction in the service for any remote community would be devastating.
Ms Spencer is the chair of remote dialysis service Purple House and said she witnesses the necessity of remote transport on a daily basis.
"Old people with renal [needs]… people want to go to funerals in communities, they don't want to get stuck here, lonely," she said.
"We want and need that bus, so people can jump in, and go to their community."

The affected routes include Santa Teresa, Atitjere-Engawala, Willowra, Hermannsberg-Areyonga and Titjikala-Finke, and Centre Bush Bus owner Tahnee Passmore-Barns said all of those routes were at risk of being cancelled altogether unless they received support.
Ms Passmore-Barns said since their funding stopped, they had been operating at a loss and had been trying to work behind the scenes to get it reinstated before going to the media this week.
"We just can't run at a loss … It's something that is quite heartbreaking for us because we have close relationships with all our communities and all our passengers," she said.
Local Aboriginal organisations and politicians have united in their calls for the service's funding to continue, citing health, safety and overcrowding concerns.
The chief executive of remote Aboriginal dialysis provider Purple House Sarah Brown said it made "no sense" to cut services.
"It would be an absolute catastrophe if the Northern Territory government lets down Bush Bus," she said.
"If there's only one Bush Bus a week, it means they're stuck in Alice Springs.
"We know that for a lot of people, they've already got more family members than the house can maintain.
"People being stuck in town in inadequate housing puts a severe pressure on that family group and their relationships."
Central Land Council chief executive Les Turner said the government had a duty to ensure people in remote places had transport options and described any funding cut as "short sighted".

"Our concern is that this is a vital arterial route for people in remote areas to access services and the service is important, which should be available to all citizens in the Northern Territory," he said.

Infrastructure Minister Bill Yan, whose electorate of Namatjira covers many of the impacted bus routes, said the service missed out on funding in 2025-26 because "they didn't meet the criteria" and "costs were not comparative with services provided in other regions" in the NT.

"The total budget for the Remote Transport Program in 2026-27 is $3.132 million, increased by $67,000 from the 2025-26 budget of $3.065 million to offset fuel and wages increases," Mr Yan said in a statement.
"We did provide a one-off time limited grant of $667,000 between October 1 and February 28 to Centre Bush Bus on five specific runs with twice weekly services for support over the summer period.
"Based on these figures, if a decision was made to extend the grant funding to 12 months, it would have cost $1.6m to service nine communities.
"This would leave around half the budget to service the other 50 communities across the Territory."
He said the funding was not designed as ongoing and the service could reapply for the grant program.
However, Centre Bush Bus is the only scheduled transport and freight service running on regular timetables to some communities.
The government has not confirmed whether any other bus companies were successful in securing a grant to cover these routes.
Labor member for the remote electorate of Gwoja Chansey Paech said this was "an absolutely pathetic excuse".
"The government heavily subsidises public transport in Darwin and Alice Springs, so why should people living in remote communities be treated any differently," he said.
Ms Passmore-Barns said increased diesel prices, long travel distances and staffing were all part of the cost of the service.
Ms Passmore-Barns said information in Mr Yan's statement about the service's cost effectiveness and having not met the criteria was new to her.

"The criteria over the last 10 or 20 years was pretty much the same, we've done dozens of applications and they've all been successful so I was actually very surprised … to be told it was not accepted was quite a shock," she said.
"Then to try and get feedback and not get any doesn't help."
She said the service was providing value for money.
"The only reason you would need funding is for those smaller communities who don't have the population to make the services sustainable," she said.
"The government even call our services essential services on their list of services in the Territory, but it doesn't look like they're essential services so much anymore."
Amid the back and forth, Marlene Spencer just hopes the services remain the same, so people can get to and from community for their health.
"Why are they talking about Bush Bus stopping? We want and need that important Bush Bus," she said.
Three men have been sentenced over the 2021 manslaughter of Carlo Stewart, with the man who sourced the gun used in the shooting given a longer sentence than the shooter.
Tye Bickle and Kobi Wilkins were handed five-year suspended sentences and were free to leave the court on parole, while Brayden Wilson-Knight was sentenced to nine years in jail.
Wilson-Knight will be eligible to apply for parole in April, 2028.
A Supreme Court judge has ruled a man who sourced the gun used to kill another man in an Ipswich brawl should spend more time in jail than the man who pulled the trigger.
In July 2021, Tye Bickle, Brayden Wilson-Knight and a teenage boy were charged with the murder of Carlo Stewart.
Mr Stewart died in hospital after suffering three gunshot wounds during a brawl between two groups outside a North Booval home.
Earlier this month the three men, now aged between 22 and 33, pleaded guilty to several charges, including a downgraded offence of manslaughter, and faced a sentencing hearing last week.
Due to how much time has passed since their arrest, the then-16-year-old boy involved was sentenced as an adult and can now be identified as Wilson-Knight's younger brother, Kobi Wilkins.
On Thursday Wilkins and Bickle were handed wholly suspended 5-year prison terms, while Wilson-Knight was jailed for nine years.
Fatal brawl sparked by stolen motorbikes
The court previously heard the fatal brawl stemmed from Mr Stewart wanting to help his friend retrieve stolen motorbikes, which had been sold to Wilson-Knight unknowingly.
Wilson-Knight planned to meet Mr Stewart in a public car park to exchange the motorbikes for cash, and he asked his brother and friend to go with him.
Instead of meeting at the arranged location, Mr Stewart decided to go to Wilson-Knight's home, and he brought several men with him, including some wearing gloves, masks and hoods.

When Wilson-Knight, who had been armed with an unregistered .22 calibre handgun, was told the group had gone there instead, where his wife and children were alone, he returned to his house with Bickle and Wilkins.
When they arrived, CCTV captured Mr Stewart saying "you boys have our bikes", before Wilson-Knight pulls the gun from his pants.
A fight broke out between the two men, and Mr Stewart told Wilson-Knight to shoot him, which he attempted to do, but the weapon did not fire.
Mr Stewart then punched Wilson-Knight in the face and armed himself with a baseball bat.
During this time, Bickle gained possession of the gun, but was immediately struck in the head with the bat by Mr Stewart which caused a serious head injury.
Bickle then fired 10 shots indiscriminately in about seven seconds, and three of the bullets connected with Mr Stewart.
Victim's mother describes him as 'lovable larrikin'
Several people provided victim impact statements to the court including Mr Stewart's mother Kay Stewart, who described her son as her "lovable larrikin".
"How can something so tragic happen to such a good-hearted person," she said in her statement.
Ms Stewart penned that "Carlo was my first love" and she has "been in hell" since his death.
"I cannot describe the pain of losing your first born … he was my everything," she said.
His partner Bonita Ruben said in her statement that Mr Stewart was a "devoted and deeply loving father figure" to her daughter, who worked hard for their family.
She wrote that Mr Stewart was "loud, energetic and larger than life" and the pain she felt when he died was "unlike anything I'd ever experienced".
Shooter was 'hurt, dazed and disoriented', judge finds
When handing down their sentences on Thursday, Justice Peter Callaghan told the court no punishment would change the "awful reality" faced by Mr Stewart's loved ones.
"The story of grief will continue to be told irrespective of anything that occurs here," he said.
Justice Callaghan acknowledged Mr Stewart and his group had been "hostile and menacing" when they deviated and went to Wilson-Knight's home and were "intent on their own brand of law enforcement".
"The momentum towards a violent encounter was gathering and became unstoppable once Mr Stewart's group changed the plan," he said.
"They must have known they had set themselves on a collision course."

He accepted Wilson-Knight would have been "horrified and frightened" by the group descending on his family home but his decision to arm himself with a loaded gun, warranted a harsher penalty to "denounce and deter" others from similar offending.
Wilson-Knight was given a head sentence of nine years in prison.
When sentencing Bickle, Justice Callaghan told the court although he was the principal offender and had "voluntarily placed himself into a potentially violent situation", his case was unique.
"This offence of manslaughter is marked by a number of features which has not been present in any other case of manslaughter dealt with by this court," he said.

He accepted Bickle had no prior knowledge of the gun, was not "proactively aggressive" in the altercation before being handed it, was severely injured and "scared and in a state of panic" when he shot Mr Stewart.
"He was hurt, dazed and disoriented," he said.
Bickle was sentenced to five years in jail wholly suspended and given immediate parole for two grievous bodily harm charges.
The same sentence was handed to Wilkins, and both men were free to leave the dock.
Their pre-sentence custody was not declared as time served, however 270 days that Wilson-Knight served on remand, was.
He will be eligible to apply for parole in April, 2028.

Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua: Rivals show respect at friendly first press conference - but how long will it last?
Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua finally came face-to-face on Wednesday - but few could have predicted how their first press conference ahead of their blockbuster heavyweight clash would unfold.

Perhaps because of the uncertainty that has continued to surround the fight since it was announced, there was something of a surreal atmosphere in west London until the two biggest names in British boxing finally appeared on stage shortly after 6pm.

The whole thing suddenly felt very real, with the audible excitement of the relatively small number of fans who had been able to buy tickets to watch from the arena's upper tier clearly appreciated by both fighters.
With the two-time world champions sat just a few feet apart, attention quickly turned to how they would interact after years of verbal sparring from a distance.
Joshua's measured persona made his approach easier to predict, but the wildcard was which version of Fury would show up.

After a lengthy introduction from master of ceremonies Max Kellerman, the American's questions about the fighters' sparring session - which took place in 2010, when Joshua was still an amateur - produced some light-hearted banter.

However, Joshua soon took control of the proceedings to pay tribute to several people in his life who had passed away, including Sina Ghami and Latif 'Latz' Ayodele, who died in a car crash in Nigeria last December that Joshua survived.
Joshua requested a minute of silence which was impeccably observed by everyone in the arena, before applause at the end of it, which Fury warmly participated in.
Whether it had always been his intention or Joshua's words had influenced him, Fury then offered some extremely kind words about his rival.
"This man is a two-time heavyweight world champion, Olympic gold medallist, and he has been a role model and a poster boy for British boxing for years," Fury said.
"I mostly find myself defending my arch rival to fans I meet in the street. If you could achieve 10 per cent of what this man has achieved, you'd be doing well."

While there is little doubt tensions will rise and less friendly exchanges will follow between now and fight night, both fighters made it clear that there is a great deal of underlying respect between them, with no obvious personal malice.
That was further underlined when Fury invited Joshua to join him for a pint of Guinness in the pub after the fight, regardless of the result.
Joshua's humorous suspicion of the invitation, however, perhaps reflected his surprise at Fury's approach to the event. Was the master of mind games at it again?
Few are better qualified to analyse this event and everything around it than Britain's former undisputed heavyweight world champion Lennox Lewis, who was in attendance.
Lewis is adamant that once Fury and Joshua are deeper into their training camps, their exchanges will become less friendly.
"It's too early, at this time [for aggro]," Lewis said. "You need to be in training camp and not see people for a couple of weeks.
"To be training hard and thinking about each other. Then when they see each other, it will be different, because everyone will be touchy at that point."

Fury also showed just how quickly he can switch from friendly to confrontational when responding to a video released by Joshua and his promoter, Eddie Hearn, before the fight was finalised. The video positioned Joshua as a 'landlord' coming to collect his money.
Fury suggested that the fact his name appears first on all the promotional material for the event proves he is the A-side of the fight.
"In the build-up to this fight, Eddie [Hearn] and AJ were talking about landlords, being the boss, being the 'guvnor', the rent man and all that," Fury said.
"When I look behind me, I only see one don and that's Fury vs AJ. Now you've come to get the rent and I ain't f****** paying because I'm No 1.
"I don't make a big thing about all that but we're going to walk out seeing Tyson Fury versus his opponent Anthony Joshua - an old dosser who works for me."
With several details still to be decided - including which fighter will walk to the ring first and be left waiting for his opponent - the battle of egos is only likely to intensify.
While the result is ultimately all that will matter, it will be fascinating to see the receptions these two legends receive in the build-up to December 11 and right through to the opening bell.
If the first press conference was anything to go by, Fury and Joshua are set to receive a huge reception wherever they go between now and fight night.
After the huge cheers that greeted both fighters as they arrived on stage, Fury's fans broke into his "get up" catchphrase, with Joshua playfully joining in and repeating it back to them.
It was also notable that there was little of the hostility often directed at one fighter by the other's supporters. Instead, the focus was firmly on backing their respective heroes.
Joshua remained on stage for at least 30 minutes after the press conference had finished, signing autographs and posing for photos with fans.
